conclusion.justification: The report concludes that while there is an observed association in observational studies, current evidence cannot reliably establish a causal link due to confounding and reverse causation biases. Thus, it treats the evidence as insufficient and gives a hedged conclusion.
conclusion.label: hedged

report:
**Conclusion: not a firm “yes” for causing Alzheimer’s/dementia.** Benzodiazepines and related “Z-drugs” are consistently associated with a higher *observed* rate of later dementia in many observational studies, especially with longer or multiple-drug exposure. But the current evidence cannot reliably establish that the medicines themselves cause Alzheimer’s disease or other dementias.

Why the uncertainty matters: insomnia, anxiety, depression, and early cognitive/behavioral changes can occur during the years before dementia is diagnosed. Those symptoms may lead to sedative prescriptions—so the drug use can be a consequence of early, undiagnosed disease (“protopathic” or reverse-causation bias), rather than its cause. A UK case-control analysis cited in a cohort-study discussion found no association with Alzheimer’s or vascular dementia after using a 3-year lag to address this bias.  
https://academic.oup.com/biomedgerontology/article/77/5/1035/6354922

An umbrella review of five meta-analyses (30 studies) found reported association estimates varied, reflecting inconsistency, heterogeneity, and bias concerns rather than conclusive causal evidence.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10608561/

Evidence for Z-drugs (for example zolpidem, zopiclone) is thinner; one cohort reported a strong association, particularly for Z-hypnotics and concurrent use of multiple agents, but this too is observational and vulnerable to confounding/reverse causation.  
https://scholar.nycu.edu.tw/en/publications/benzodiazepines-z-hypnotics-and-risk-of-dementia-special-consider

Regardless of dementia causation, these drugs can cause acute cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, and fractures in older adults. The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria therefore recommends avoiding benzodiazepines in older adults when possible.  
https://www.ncqa.org/report-cards/health-plans/state-of-health-care-quality-report/deprescribing-of-benzodiazepines-in-older-adults-dbo/

Do not stop a regular benzodiazepine abruptly; discuss a supervised taper and alternatives with the prescriber.
